verses.note: The first mention of public prayer in Scripture stands at the end of a chapter of violence. Calling on the LORD's name is presented as the mark of the line that God preserves, the phrase Joel and Paul use of those who will be saved (Joel 2:32, Romans 10:13).
Abram's life in the land is marked by public worship. Calling on the LORD's name at an altar, where others could see it, declares whose land this is and whose protection he trusts.

The text records no altar and no calling on the LORD's name in Egypt. Its return here, at the same spot as before, suggests that Abram's life with God is being resumed after a lapse. Many interpreters read it as a return in the sense of repentance, though the text does not use that word.

Abram's first recorded words to God are not praise but complaint, and God answers with a fuller promise rather than a rebuke. The lament psalms follow the same pattern: honest speech to God is itself an act of faith.
The text records no prayer from Hagar, only her affliction, and God is said to hear it. Scripture presents suffering itself as something that reaches God, as Israel's groaning does in Exodus 2:23-25.
Abraham's first recorded prayer for another person is for Ishmael. God does not grant it in the form asked, but he hears it (verse 20), and the answer is generous.

Abraham's prayer is an argument from God's own justice. He does not ask God to be less just but to act consistently with his justice, which makes this chapter a model for prayer that appeals to God's character.
Boldness and humility grow together in Abraham's prayer. He dares more precisely because he confesses that he is dust, and God does not rebuke him for it.

God grants every request Abraham makes. The limit of the conversation is set by Abraham's asking, not by God's willingness, which is why many readers take the chapter as an invitation to pray for more than one dares.
Lot's plea echoes Abraham's intercession in form, with its polite formulas and its bargaining, but its subject is only himself. The contrast shows what chapter 18 is about: Abraham asked for others.
Abraham never asked for Lot by name, and ten righteous men were not found. God still answered the heart of the prayer, that the righteous not be swept away with the wicked.

The first mention of prayer with this verb is intercession: one person asking God on behalf of another. It is a prophet's work, and the pattern continues through Moses (Numbers 21:7), Samuel (1 Samuel 12:23), and Job (Job 42:8).

The prayer that heals comes from the man who caused the harm. God answers because he appointed Abraham to pray, not because Abraham has earned a hearing, and the result is life for a household outside the covenant.
No prayer is recorded, only a voice, and God hears it. The verse gives the ground for every cry that has no words: God listens where the one crying lies.

The servant's prayer is specific, humble, and grounded in God's commitment to someone else. He asks not for his own sake but for his master's, appealing to God's chesed. Prayer here is an act of dependence in the middle of an ordinary task.
God answers before the request is complete, the pattern Isaiah 65:24 states as promise and Daniel 9:20-23 describes as experience. The answer was already on its way when the servant began to pray.
Thanksgiving follows the answer immediately and is spoken aloud before anyone else. The servant's prayer life has two movements in one scene: asking (verses 12-14) and blessing (verse 27).

The promise of descendants was sworn to Abraham and certain, yet Isaac still prays for it. The verse teaches that God's promises do not make prayer unnecessary; they are what gives prayer its ground, and God's fulfilment arrives through it.

Rebekah brings her confusion straight to God, not only her request. Scripture treats that kind of honest question as a form of seeking God, and she receives an answer that explains her suffering without removing it.
God's word to Isaac is answered with worship before anything else. The order of the verse, altar, then tent, then well, is the order of a life that puts calling on God before securing its own needs.
Jacob's vow is a prayer that asks God to do what God has just said he will do. However mixed Jacob's motives, the form is sound: the promises of God are what a person has to hold God to.

Jacob does everything he can (gifts, double silver, the brother) and then prays for what he cannot do: that God would change the heart of a foreign ruler. His prayer is answered in the very man he fears, whose compassion, rachamim, will grow warm for Benjamin in verse 30.
